name: Mittelniederländisch
confidence_why: Franck 1910 and Schönfeld and van Loey 1970 both give Middle Dutch the Germanic root-syllable accent (first syllable of simple words, the verb root in prefixed verbs) and Fikkert's metrical studies of the Lutgart (1998, 2000) confirm main stress on the initial root foot, so the one dissent, Zonneveld 1993's claim that the Lutgart already shows Modern Dutch right-edge stress, rests on Romance loans and heavy final syllables and leaves the root stress of native words untouched.

sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title, Fikkert 1998 (Linguistics in the Netherlands 15, open access, already held by the project and already in our bibliography): read in full. It is a first-hand metrical analysis of the 13th-c. 'Sente Lutgart' and states that stress in Middle Dutch was still mainly initial/root (Germanic foot, left-to-right, main stress on the initial foot), with prefixed words stressing the root, native suffixes unstressed, and two systematic deviations: stress shift to a branching second foot in (H)(HL) words and retained final stress in superheavy-final Romance loans. This refines rather than contradicts the catalog's 'morphological' coding from Franck 1910 §10; Fikkert herself cites Franck 1910 and Schönfeld as the grammars stating mainly-initial stress. I do not recommend replacing Franck as the deciding source (his statement is the general grammar rule; Fikkert is a single-text analysis), but Fikkert should be cited alongside as the modern, evidence-based refinement, with a note on quantity sensitivity and loanword final stress. Two further texts already held by the project from the 9/16 download were also read: Zonneveld 1993 (Spektator 22, DBNL) argues the 13th-c. system was already modern-Dutch-like (penultimate before open finals, final on superheavies) but concedes the evidence cannot settle window or quantity sensitivity, and is rebutted by Fikkert; Schönfeld 1970 §88 (DBNL) confirms the root-syllable doctrine with a Middle Dutch example. Nothing remains to acquire

new_statements.quote: p. 114: "In this section we consider the prosodic variation in 'Lutgart' from the viewpoint of the early WGmc prosodic system, i.e. the foot is the Germanic foot; feet are built from left to right; main stress falls on the initial foot, and final non-branching feet are defooted." p. 121: "In this paper I have argued that the word stress system at the time of 'Lutgart' was not the same as that of modern Dutch, but was more similar to that of the other West Germanic languages in the old and middle period; i.e. the Germanic foot was still prevalent."
new_statements.citation: Fikkert, Paula. 1998. Foot Structure and Word Stress in Middle Dutch: Evidence from 'Lutgart'. Linguistics in the Netherlands 15, 109-122. DOI 10.1075/avt.15.11fik
new_statements.locator: p. 114 (§5, PDF page 6) and p. 121 (§7 Conclusions, PDF page 13)
new_statements.reading: Middle Dutch of c. 1265 has main stress on the leftmost (initial/root) foot of a left-to-right quantity-sensitive Germanic-foot parse: native words are initial/root-stressed, native suffixes do not take stress, prefixed words stress the root, LH(L) words (coninc, coninge) are invariably initial. The departures are prosodic and lexical: (H)(HL) words shift main stress to the heavier second foot (ambáchte, uiánde), and Romance loans with superheavy final syllables keep final stress (tormént, parloer, latijn). This is consistent with the catalog's 'morphological' (root-syllable) coding from Franck 1910 §10 and adds a weight-sensitive component that Franck's statement lacks; it explicitly rejects Zonneveld's (1993) claim that the system was already modern-Dutch right-edge stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's root-syllable (Franck 1910 §10 'morphological') coding and with the existing Fikkert 1998 statement: this chapter is the full-length version of the 1998 Linguistics Library paper on the same 'Lutgart' data. It adds detail beyond both: the weight-driven shift to a branching second foot, the (H)(H) variation and its line-position conditioning, the exceptionless final stress of superheavy Romance loans, secondary stress on strong native suffixes, and the argument that Open Syllable Lengthening had not yet applied (coninc/coninge invariably initial). It contradicts only Zonneveld 1993 (right-edge, Modern-Dutch-like stress), which is not what the catalog records.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Early Middle Dutch (the Brabantine 'Lutgart', c. 1263-1270) still has the West Germanic system: main stress on the first syllable of the root (initial for unprefixed words, root-initial for prefixed words, both nouns and verbs), feet being the quantity-sensitive Germanic Foot (VV and VC both heavy) built left to right with main stress on the leftmost foot and destressing of final non-branching feet. Departures are prosodic and lexical: in (H)(HL) words (ambáchte, uiánde, uonnésse) main stress shifts to the heavier branching second foot; (H)(H) words vary (initial preferred, final obligatory line-finally); Romance loans with superheavy final syllables (tormént, parlóer, latijn, procés) invariably keep final stress; LH(L) words like coninc/coninge are invariably initial because OSL had not yet applied. Fikkert explicitly rejects Zonneveld's (1992, 1993a, 1998) conclusion that the 'Lutgart' system was already Modern-Dutch right-edge stress (main stress on one of the last three syllables).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Strong native derivational suffixes (-doem, -heit, -lijk, -scap, -kijn, -linc, -âre, -ech, -inghe, -inc, -ich, -nisse) 'according to many authors (cf. Franck 1910: section 11; Le Roux and Le Roux 1969) always carried secondary accent' (p. 319) and in 'Lutgart' invariably keep main stress on the root/first foot; native superheavy suffixes 'bore at least secondary stress' (p. 304); the main-stressed foot prefers to be at least as complex as secondary-stressed feet (pp. 315-316, 327).
new_statements.exceptions: (H)(HL) words shift main stress to the branching second foot (ambáchte, uiánde, bispéle, uonnésse, blischápen; also suffix + inflection, e.g. ermínge); (H)(H) words vary between initial and final (ambacht/ambácht, viant/viánt, orlof/orlóf), final stress being obligatory line-finally; Romance loans with superheavy final syllables invariably final-stressed (tormént, pulmént, consént, sermóen, parlóer, jordáen, latijn, procés, paradijs); Zonneveld's list of penultimate stress in vowel-final loans (grácie, glórie, senténtie) with exceptions baillú, Golgathá; the word ermíne as the one exception among native suffixed (H)(H) words; prefixed words stress the root with no noun/verb difference (mesdáet, ónrecht cited as root-stressed in Lutgart, unlike Modern Dutch ónrecht).
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter describes the language of one text: the 'Copenhagen Lutgart' (Sente Lutgart, books 2-3), a Brabantine Middle Dutch rhymed poem written c. 1263-1270, probably by Willem van Affligem (born Mechelen); the manuscript originates in Brabant. Claims are about early Middle Dutch of that period and region, contrasted throughout with Modern Dutch and with the handbook accounts of Middle Dutch generally (Franck 1910, Schönfeld 1947, Van Bree 1977/1987).

readall_conflicts: The one opened work agrees with the catalog and the existing Fikkert 1998 statement. The only disagreement in the literature is the one the chapter itself argues against: Zonneveld (1992, 1993a, 1998), previously downloaded into this folder as zonneveld1993_spektator22, holds that 'Lutgart' already had the Modern Dutch right-to-left, right-edge stress system (main stress on one of the last three syllables, schwa as stress attractor), whereas Fikkert 2000 argues stress was still assigned from the left with main stress on the root-initial foot, variation being due to foot complexity ((H)(HL) preferring the branching second foot) and to superheavy Romance loans keeping final stress. The two agree on the surface facts for vowel-final loans (penultimate) and for superheavy-final loans (final).

sources.citation: Fikkert, Paula. 1998. Foot Structure and Word Stress in Middle Dutch: Evidence from 'Lutgart'. Linguistics in the Netherlands 15, 109-122. AVT Publications.
sources.quote: p. 110: "Stress was by and large initial in WGmc. Most MNL grammars mention that stress was still mainly initial, and attribute non-initial word stress to three different groups of words (cf. Schönfeld 1947, Franck 1910, van Bree 1977, 1987). First, prefixed verbs have word stress on the root, resulting in non-initial word stress. Second, certain suffixes (mostly native ones) attract stress to the syllable immediately preceding the suffix, as in driehoek — driehoekig ('triangle' — 'triangular'). Third, loan words maintain main stress in their original position."
sources.note: Corpus-metrical study of the 13th-c. iambic poem 'Sente Lutgart' (Brabant, c. 1263-70). Fikkert assumes and argues for the early West Germanic system: Germanic (resolved moraic) trochee, feet built left to right, main stress on the initial foot, final non-branching feet defooted (p. 114). Native words are root/initial-stressed; words with strong native suffixes (-heit, -scap, -lijk, -nisse, -inghe..) sources.citation: Schönfeld, M. (bew. A. van Loey). 1970. Historische grammatica van het Nederlands. 8th ed. Zutphen: Thieme. Derde hoofdstuk, I. Het accent, §§ 87-88.
sources.quote: §88: "al spoedig, nog in gemeengerm. tijd, werd de klemtoon vooraan overheersend ... Daar nu in de regel de stamsyllabe de eerste was, kreeg deze gewoonlijk de hoofdtoon; m.a.w. de dynamische accentuatie werd in hoofdzaak een logische. ... Toen de klemverschuiving plaats had, had men in 't ogm. nog geen samengestelde w.w., vandaar dat deze in tegenstelling tot de nominale composita de klemtoon op het tweede lid hebben ... ndl. verzórgen: vóorzorg, weerstaán: wéerstand, belúiken: mnl. bíloke 'klooster'" [Tr.: soon, still in Common Germanic, initial stress became dominant ... Since the stem syllable was as a rule the first, it usually received the main stress; i.e. dynamic accentuation became essentially a logical (root-based) one ... When the stress shift happened, Old Germanic had no compound verbs yet, hence these, unlike nominal compounds, stress the second member ... Du. verzórgen : vóorzorg, weerstaán : wéerstand, belúiken : MDu. bíloke 'monastery'.]
sources.note: General historical grammar of Dutch (covering Middle Dutch): Germanic main stress on the stem (root) syllable, normally the first; prefixed verbs stress the root (second member), nominal compounds the first member, with a Middle Dutch example (bíloke). Same doctrine as the catalog's Franck 1910 §10.

sources.citation: Schönfeld, M. (bewerkt door A. van Loey). 1970. Historische grammatica van het Nederlands, 8e druk. Zutphen: Thieme. Hoofdstuk 3 'Het accent', §§87-90. (DBNL full text)
sources.quote: §88: Germanic fixed the main accent on the first (= stem) syllable; compound verbs, unlike nominal compounds, stress the second member (verzórgen : vóorzorg, weerstaán : wéerstand, belúiken : mnl. bíloke). §89: 'In het ndl. is, in principe, het beginaccent van het ogm. bewaard gebleven', with later rhythmic/analogical shifts, e.g. suffixes -ig, -lijk, -baar, -zaam attracting accent to the preceding syllable. General Dutch diachrony rather than MNL-specific, but the same rule set as Franck §10-11.
